cia-0000119751: Current as of 5 p.m. on November 6, 1956, this CIA report gives the Hungarian situation two days into the Soviet crackdown. Organized resistance was failing across the country. cia-0000132651:
The growth of Cuba's armed forces fills a CIA paper dated January 4, 1961. Three months before the Bay of Pigs landing, the island was arming fast. Weapons from the Soviet bloc were arriving by the shipload through that winter.

The paper measures the buildup in men, guns, and new units. Such counts shaped the plans of the exile force then training for the invasion. For readers, the entry shows the military balance as the agency saw it in the new year. Both sides were racing, and the paper records one side of that race in detail.
cia-0000134251: North Korea and Cuba setting up formal ties fill a CIA paper dated August 4, 1960. Pyongyang and Havana made an odd pair on the map of the Cold War. Their friendship would last for decades once the embassies opened. Two revolutions were making their bond official that summer. The short paper notes the step and the statements that went with it.
cia-0000136051: A CIA cable dated 1 February 1954 deals with a request to stick to plans and general conditions, the condition that follows cut off, in files since declassified. cia-0000136351: Congratulations from headquarters, received through ASCHAM, are passed down the line in this early July 1954 LINCOLN cable. A great victory has been won in the past forty-eight hours, the message says, made more notable by the extreme difficulties and the odds recognized against success from the outset. The energy and devotion of personnel at LINCOLN and the field stations were truly exceptional. Officers are told to pass the credit to the field, where it was earned.
un-ga-res-a-69-51:
The illicit trade in small arms fuels wars far from any factory, and Resolution A/69/51, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, renews the world plan against it. The text recalls the vote of the year before, and the first of the chain, passed on Christmas Eve 2001. At its heart stands the Programme of Action of 2001, the world deal to bar, fight, and wipe out the illicit trade in small arms and light weapons.

Full work on that plan is pressed as a must. So is work on its twin, the world tracing tool of 2005, which lets states mark arms and track the illicit ones fast and with trust. States had pledged themselves to both plans at past review meetings, and the vote holds them to it.
un-sc-res-1451: Filed in the official record under number 1451, this Council resolution is catalogued with a 2002 date. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1751: Resolution 1751, from 2007, records a Security Council decision in the official wording held by English Wikisource. The document's structure is disciplined: what the members recalled, what they noted, and then what they decided, in numbered steps. Preserving that structure is preserving the decision, which is the work this entry does for later readers in this collection.
cia-0000132751: A same-day companion to other January 4, 1961 Cuba briefings, this CIA paper reflects the view from just after the diplomatic break. The United States had cut ties with Havana the day before, and the agency filed several papers at once to fix the new baseline. The declassified companion piece survives through the CIA Reading Room mirror at the Internet Archive.
cia-0000135751: The 2506 Brigade files hold this Spanish-language document under an estimated date of 1 January 1961, flagged as estimated in the catalog title itself. The brigade was the CIA's exile force, then in winter training for Cuba. No subject is recorded for the item. It survives in Spanish in the declassified release. plos-pone-0000051:
Yoshitake Sano, Tadashi Nakaya, Steve Pedrini, and co-authors tested a suspected cause of Alzheimer's disease chemistry in a 2006 paper. The amyloid precursor protein, APP, is cut to make the A-beta fragments that pile up in Alzheimer's brains. Adding a phosphate at one site on APP, threonine-668, was thought to drive that cutting in the living brain.

Measuring normal mouse brains, the team found physiological A-beta levels are not related to that phosphorylation state. A negative result can be as useful as a positive one. It steers drug hunters away from a target that does not govern A-beta under normal conditions. It also sharpens the search for what does.
cia-0000137451:
South Vietnamese Liberation Army Enemy Proselyting Office Handling of Prisoners, dated 1971, is a declassified CIA report from the Vietnam War. Its title names its subject in full: how the enemy's proselyting office, the unit charged with winning over captives, handled prisoners it held. Proselyting here means political persuasion work aimed at prisoners of war.

Reports of this kind served a practical purpose. Knowing how captives were treated, and how they were pressed to change sides, shaped briefings for troops and the care of men who came home. The 1971 date places the report in the war's later years, when American forces were drawing down but prisoners remained a live and painful issue.
cia-0000139451: Remote viewing, the attempt to gather intelligence by claimed psychic sight, fills document 0000139451 from Project SUN STREAK in 1988. The program ran under defense and intelligence sponsorship through the 1980s, with viewers set targets they could not see and their reports scored for hits. Nothing in this record sets it apart from the program's general run of files. Freed with the rest of the SUN STREAK archive, it helps show how far officials once went for an edge.
un-sc-res-351:
Security Council Resolution 351, adopted on June 10, 1974, recommended Bangladesh for membership in the United Nations. Bangladesh had broken from Pakistan in 1971 after a war marked by mass killing and a vast flight of refugees. Its first bid for a seat had met a Chinese veto in 1972, cast in support of Pakistan; by 1974 the path had cleared.

Pakistan itself had come to accept Bangladesh, and the Assembly seated the new state that September. The resolution is short and formal, yet it closed one of the sorest disputes left from the partition of British India. Bangladesh took its place as one of the world's most populous nations.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d51: Roosevelt wrote to Churchill on October 21, 1943, the same day he exchanged letters with Hull in Moscow. The message is Document 51 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Running two channels at once, one to his minister and one to his ally, was the president's normal method that autumn. The record names no subject for this letter. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series among the Moscow Conference papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d151: Patrick Hurley, the President's personal representative, wrote to Roosevelt on November 20, 1943, and the report is Document 151 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Hurley traveled widely on the president's errands in the Middle East and Asia, and his blunt reports were a known White House taste. The record gives the date and the two men and no subject. The report is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d251:
An editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume covers an informal evening gathering at Cairo on 22 November 1943, for which no minutes were taken or have been found. The time and the names of those present come from the President's Log, and the editors piece the purpose together from three published accounts.

Admiral Leahy records that the Combined Chiefs joined the President's dinner party after the meal. Lord Mountbatten laid out his plans and needs for the Burma campaign assigned to him at Quebec. General Alanbrooke calls the aim a discussion of Mountbatten's plans to prepare for meetings with Chiang Kai-shek. The editors doubt the Chinese party listed in the Log actually attended.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d351:
Harry Hopkins telegraphed Steve Early, the President's secretary, from Tehran on 2 December 1943, fixing the release of the next conference statement. Sent by military channels, the short message looks ahead to the Tehran communiqué and back at the troubled Cairo release.

The Tehran text, Hopkins states, will be released for publication at one in the afternoon, Washington time, and eight in the evening, Moscow time, on 6 December. The details of the release are to follow. He also asks Early to send a report on how the Chinese communiqué was handled. The report should include any breaches of the release date. It should cover any unauthorized early publication of facts about the Cairo or Tehran conferences. Early's suggestions for doing better are asked for as well.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d451:
December 6, 1943 was the closing day of the Second Cairo Conference, and the Combined Chiefs of Staff held a session whose minutes the State Department printed in its Cairo-Tehran volume. The chiefs were the senior American and British officers charged with running the two countries' common war effort. Their Cairo work followed directly from the Tehran meeting with Stalin.

Final-day minutes tend to gather up loose ends: last decisions recorded, reports noted, and conclusions readied for Roosevelt and Churchill before the delegations scattered. For the reader, this record closes the military story of the conference. It shows the machinery of alliance settling its business before the leaders went home.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d551:
Marshal Stalin addressed a joint message to President Roosevelt and Prime Minister Churchill on January 29, 1944. Stalin usually wrote to the two leaders separately, so a message to both at once marked business he wanted the whole alliance to hear. It appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

The three-way partnership rested on constant reporting among the capitals, and a joint message from Moscow carried the weight of the partner who was doing most of the fighting that winter. The Red Army's offensives were then driving the Germans back across Ukraine. For readers, the document shows Stalin speaking to the Western leaders together, as Tehran had briefly made them.
frus-1944-quebec-d51:
Representatives of the British Chiefs of Staff prepared a memorandum on September 2, 1944. They worked in Washington. Their mission kept London's military positions current with the American chiefs. Gaps between summits made that work constant. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Ten days before Quebec, staff papers lined up the military questions. Officers framed choices about the final drive into Germany. They also framed the war in Burma and the Pacific. Force sharing between the allies needed decisions too. Missions in Washington did that lining up daily. For readers, the memorandum shows professional preparation behind the conference. Chiefs would later argue the choices their officers framed.
frus-1944-quebec-d151:
In Scaf 78, dated September 9, 1944, Eisenhower gave the Combined Chiefs a brief situation report and a full statement of his intentions in France. Northern France and much of Belgium were liberated, his troops had entered Holland, and Seventh Army was about to join the central armies. Against that, German-held Schelde islands would delay using Antwerp's port.

His intention was to press on with all speed, destroy the German armed forces, and occupy Germany's heart. The main effort would breach the Siegfried Line toward the Ruhr, with the Saar as the second thrust. An airborne operation to seize Rhine crossings near Arnhem and Nijmegen awaited only good weather. Capturing the Ruhr and Saar, he argued, would strangle Germany's war industry.
frus-1944-quebec-d251:
Stettinius reported a deadlock, and a possible way through it, to Roosevelt on September 14, 1944. Ambassador Gromyko had received his instructions from Moscow on voting in the proposed Security Council. The Soviet government maintained its insistence on the inviolability of the unanimity of the four great powers. On that point, Gromyko said, there was no possibility of his being authorized to give in.

Working with the British and Russians, Stettinius had devised a compromise formula. In procedures for pacific settlement of disputes, the votes of council members party to a dispute would not be counted. In enforcement action, decisions would require the concurrence of the permanent members, including parties. Gromyko was sounding out his government, and Stettinius asked for the president's views as promptly as possible.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d51: From Moscow on 11 January 1945, Harriman sent Roosevelt a report that stands as document 51. It belongs to the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences, issued by the Department of State. Written three weeks before Yalta opened, the report helped the president judge what the Soviet leadership might demand, and what it might accept, once talks began.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d151:
Relations with the London Poles would be no more than “correct,” Stettinius cabled Harriman on 13 December 1944. His secret and urgent instruction, number 2828, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It sets the line Harriman was to hold in Moscow on Poland.

The present Polish cabinet, Washington judged, could not work out any agreement with the Soviet government. Ambassador Lane would stay in Washington until January, and no meaning was to be read into that. Harriman was to make clear that the United States still recognizes the London government. If it helped, he could add that Washington would not look kindly on Soviet recognition of the Lublin Committee. Should the London cabinet fall, Mikolajczyk might yet form one that backed his own policy.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d251:
Harriman arranged a Friday meeting to draw Stalin out on the Pacific war. His report to the President of 11 October 1944, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, describes the plan agreed with Churchill the night before. Presidential approval was still to come.

Stalin and his military men would face Churchill, Brooke, Ismay, Deane, and Harriman. The chief aim is to learn two things. How soon after Germany's collapse will Stalin be ready to act against Japan? And what, in general, can Russia bring to that war? The picture gained would clear the way for the detailed talks between Deane and the Red Army Staff. Those, Harriman insists, should be Soviet-American only, with the British kept informed.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d351:
Of this meeting, nothing said survives at all. The editors' note reports that no record of its substance has been found in the files. What is known of the session — its time and who attended — comes from the official trip log alone. The log shows the talks went on after lunch until 3 p.m.

Gaps like this run through the Yalta record, and the volume marks them rather than hiding them. A reader learns where the paper trail ends. Whatever passed between the leaders that afternoon stayed with the men in the room. The note stands as a warning against over-reading the famous record.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d451:
Agreement on Poland leads Eden's report in Bohlen's minutes of the plenary of February 10, 1945. Eden told the leaders the foreign ministers had settled the future government of Poland. Two questions within it he would refer to later. He then read the new formula, with one correction he admitted Molotov had made.

A new situation, the formula begins, has been created by Poland's complete liberation by the Red Army. A Polish provisional government, more broadly based, must follow. The session's list runs on: French participation in Germany's control commission, Yugoslavia, the world body, reparations, and the Dardanelles. Bohlen records the conference reaching its harvest day.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d51:
President Truman settled the argument over dates in a top secret reply to Churchill on June 5, 1945. The message is document 51 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference, answering Churchill's plea for an earlier Big Three meeting. Only part of the telegram is printed, but its decision is complete.

Truman says that after full consideration, July 15 is the earliest date he can manage. Plans are therefore going ahead for him to travel to the area near Berlin and arrive on that day. Churchill had warned that delay would let Soviet power harden in central Europe, but the President held firm. The exchange fixed the opening date of the Potsdam Conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d151:
Churchill showed Truman his reply to Stalin about the Balkan states in telegram number 83, sent June 10, 1945. The message is document 151 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Stalin had written on May 27 that the time had come to restore diplomatic relations with Romania, Bulgaria, and Finland, and perhaps soon with Hungary.

Churchill's quoted reply thanks Stalin for the news. Britain has been weighing its own future relations with those states, he writes, and hopes very shortly to put full proposals before Stalin and the United States government. He hopes the three can then discuss them when they next meet. The exchange touched a sore point: the ex-enemy states of Eastern Europe were falling under Soviet control, and recognition was one lever the West still held.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d251:
A briefing paper set American aims on Soviet support for the Cairo Declaration, in extracts dated June 29, 1945. The paper is document 251 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It formed part of the annexes to the State Department's agenda memorandum for the President.

The minimum objective is to win Soviet adherence to the Cairo Declaration. That would give Moscow's backing to the pledge that Korea in due course shall be free and independent. It would also bar any one power from setting up a friendly government on its own in the territories concerned. The maximum objective goes further: an agreement among the three powers, with China's expected cooperation, to jointly support the measures best suited to grow a strong, democratic, independent Korean nation. The full text appears later in the volume.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d351:
German central offices form the third topic in Dunn's extracts of his July 14, 1945 talk with Sir Alexander Cadogan at Potsdam. Cadogan cited a memorandum by Field Marshal Montgomery, approved by the Prime Minister. It urged restoring central German ministries so the Control Council could handle problems that touched Germany as a whole.

Cadogan doubted Berlin could house such agencies. Dunn answered that the United States favored building German central administrative agencies, though under a less imposing title than ministries. The exchange shows both allies groping toward the same need: some German machine, under allied control, to run railways, food, and finance across zone lines.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d451:
MacVeagh's letter to Prime Minister Voulgaris, written at Athens on July 13, 1945, carries the Greek election proposal to the Greek government itself. Under his instructions, he informs the Premier of allied obligations to Greece, the undertakings at Yalta, and Article Nine of the Varkiza Agreement. America and Britain have agreed on a joint step.

If the move is agreeable to the Royal Hellenic Government, the two powers will approach the Soviet Union and France. Their proposal: that the approaching Greek national elections be held under the supervision of the four allies named. Voulgaris returned the letter at once, with his signed agreement written on it that same morning.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d551:
A top secret briefing paper on Yugoslavia was drawn up for the Potsdam Conference on July 5, 1945. It is document 551 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers. Its subject is how Marshal Tito had dealt with the Crimea, or Yalta, pledges on his country.

The paper says Tito has not carried out those pledges. A regency and a joint government were set up in March 1945 under the Tito-Subasic deal. But the wartime assembly was never widened as promised, and six new federal states are all run by partisans. It cites seized property, attacks on clergy, and U.S. firms put under state control. It urges the three powers to restate the pledges and offer to consult.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d651:
A top secret briefing paper on the future of the Tangier zone was dated June 29, 1945. It is document 651 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Tangier, in Morocco, had been run under an international statute since 1923.

hawthorne-wonder-book-1851:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published A Wonder-Book for Girls and Boys in 1851, his retelling of Greek myths. The book fixed the classical myths in the Anglophone imagination for generations of young readers everywhere. Hawthorne wrote it fast, for money, and it became his most popular book in his lifetime.

Student Eustace Bright tells six myths to children at Tanglewood, in the Berkshire hills of Massachusetts. Perseus slays Medusa, Midas turns his child to gold, and Hercules and Pandora fill the set. Hawthorne softens the myths' cruelty and pagan edge for the nursery without killing their wonder and strangeness. His frame of child listeners keeps the old tales warm, present, and full of questions. The book set the pattern for children's myth retellings in English ever since.
hawthorne-snow-image-1851:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published The Snow-Image, and Other Twice-Told Tales in 1851, a full story collection. The volume holds famed tales like The Great Stone Face and Ethan Brand among its pieces. It gathers his later magazine work into the last tale book of his lifetime in print.

A father shapes a snow child who cannot live in a warm room by the fire. A lime-burner hunts the Unpardonable Sin and finds it in his own cold, watchful heart at last. The Great Stone Face teaches a valley poet to match the profile he reveres on the mountain. Hawthorne mixes whimsy and dread, children and sinners, in tales of rare finish and quiet power here. The collection rounds out the story art that first made his American name.
ruskin-stones-venice-vol-1-1851:
John Ruskin published The Stones of Venice, Volume 1, in 1851, subtitled The Foundations. Ruskin studies Venetian buildings as records of moral and social life. This volume lays out the elements of architecture: walls, roofs, openings, and ornament. He judges each form by truth to nature and to its materials.

Ruskin praises Gothic craft against the machine-made work of his own century. Imperfection, for him, is a sign of free and living labor. The book began his campaign to remake English taste. Architects and reformers took its lessons to heart. It remains a founding text of the Arts and Crafts spirit.
spencer-social-statics-1851:
Herbert Spencer published Social Statics in 1851, his first statement of a social system. The book sets out the law of equal freedom. Each person, Spencer argues, may do as he wills so long as he does not infringe the equal freedom of others. From that law he derives rights to property, speech, and trade.

He opposes state churches, state education, and state poor relief as breaches of the law. Land ownership receives a radical chapter that he later softened. The book became a bible of classical liberalism in its strictest form. Later Spencer revised some claims, yet the core principle endured. It remains his most quoted early work.
finney-systematic-theology-1851:
Finney's Lectures on Systematic Theology, published in 1851, give the Oberlin evangelist's complete doctrinal system in his own words. Finney taught theology at Oberlin College in Ohio, where his revival preaching had already reshaped American evangelical life. The lectures were his classroom teaching, set down in full.

His system is known as moral-government theology: God rules as a moral governor, and sinners can repent because the will is truly free. Finney argues point by point against the stricter Calvinism in which he had been raised. The book remains the fullest statement of Oberlin theology and of revivalist doctrine.
glauber-furni-novi-philosophici-1651:
Johann Rudolf Glauber published Furni Novi Philosophici in 1651, a work on new philosophical furnaces. Glauber was a German-Dutch chemist known for Glauber's salt and for skill with furnaces and distillation. Better ovens, he argued, meant better chemical work.

Designs and directions show how to build furnaces and use them to draw spirits, oils, and salts from many materials. Glauber treated wine, metals, plants, and minerals, and he hinted at uses in medicine and trade. He guarded some secrets while printing enough to prove his skill. The book captures a moment when craft knowledge of fire and vessels was becoming modern chemistry.
oviedo-historia-general-natural-vol-1-18:
Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo, the Spanish crown's official chronicler of the Indies, began his Historia general y natural de las Indias in 1535. The work ran on to 1557, and volume one here follows the Royal Academy of History edition printed at Madrid from 1851 to 1855. The text is in Spanish, as no public-domain English translation exists.

Oviedo had lived in the Americas and wrote as both historian and naturalist. His first volume opens the general history of the discoveries and the natural wonders of the New World. Plants, animals, and peoples new to Europe fill his pages. The Historia became the first natural history of the Americas, and a base source for all later study.
oviedo-historia-general-natural-vol-2-18:
Volume two of Oviedo's Historia general y natural de las Indias continues the work Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo pursued from 1535 to 1557. The Royal Academy of History edition, Madrid, 1851 to 1855, supplies the Spanish text. Oviedo wrote as the crown's own chronicler, charged with recording the lands Spain had seized across the ocean.

His history joins the story of conquest to a survey of nature in the New World. The plants, beasts, and customs he describes were marvels to his first readers in Spain. Modern scholars mine these volumes for early sightings of American life, human and wild. Volume two carries that double record forward, part chronicle and part field guide.
oviedo-historia-general-natural-vol-3-18:
The third volume of the Historia general y natural de las Indias keeps Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo's great survey moving. Oviedo, official chronicler to the Spanish crown, worked on the Historia from 1535 to 1557. This volume follows the Royal Academy of History edition of Madrid, 1851 to 1855, in the original Spanish.

By this stage the work's twin aims stand plain: tell the deeds of the conquerors, and catalogue the nature of the Indies. Oviedo describes lands and peoples from his own years in America and from reports he trusted. His pages preserve early European knowledge of American plants and animals found nowhere else. The third volume is a working part of that first natural history.
oviedo-historia-general-natural-vol-4-18:
Volume four completes the Royal Academy of History edition of Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo's Historia general y natural de las Indias. The edition ran at Madrid from 1851 to 1855, in Spanish. Oviedo's own labor on the Historia stretched from 1535 to 1557, as the Spanish crown's appointed chronicler of the New World.

The closing volume carries his record of conquest and nature to its end. Oviedo writes as a man who crossed the ocean, governed, planted, and observed for decades. His natural history gave Europe its first broad account of American species and landscapes. His chronicle, proud and partisan, remains a source no student of the conquest can skip. The set closes with its witness still speaking.
hume-enquiry-principles-morals-1751:
Hume called An Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals, from 1751, his own favorite among his works. Nine sections, two appendices, and a closing Dialogue make up the book. Its question is plain: why do we praise some traits of character and blame others, in every age and land?

Hume's answer is the moral-sense theory in its ripest form. We approve what is useful or agreeable, to ourselves or to others, and sentiment, guided by reason, does the approving. Benevolence, justice, and politeness all fall under his calm survey. The Enquiry reads more smoothly than any other of his books. It remains a founding text of modern moral philosophy.
hobbes-de-cive-1651:
Thomas Hobbes published De Cive in Latin in 1642, and the English translation of 1651 gives it as Philosophical Rudiments Concerning Government and Society. Three parts treat liberty, dominion, and religion in turn. The book stands between his Elements of Law and the Leviathan of 1651, where his political philosophy reached its famous form.

Hobbes argues that men in nature, without a common power, live in fear and war. Peace requires a sovereign set up by covenant, whose commands are law. Religion, in the third part, must answer to that sovereign within his realm. De Cive states the case more briefly than Leviathan, and scholars prize its clarity.
gregory-letters-candid-inquirer-1851:
William Gregory systematized animal magnetism in Letters to a Candid Inquirer, printed in 1851. Gregory, a chemist at Edinburgh, wrote the letters as a manual for the open minded. Magnetic sleep, clairvoyance, and mesmeric cure receive ordered treatment. He gathers the evidence claim by claim, with cases in support.

The book became the standard British manual of the subject for mid Victorian readers. Through it, many households first met mesmerism in sober form. Gregory answers doubters while granting the field its share of fraud. His order and calm made the strange seem studyable. The letters preserve how Britain learned mesmerism. They remain a clear window on the practice.
zoist-vol-09-1851:
March 1851 to January 1852 is the span of The Zoist's ninth volume. The Great Exhibition year finds Elliotson still editing his journal of mesmerism. Painless operations, trance cures, and clairvoyant sittings fill the reports. Cerebral physiology articles continue the journal's scientific frame.

Spiritualism, newly landed from America, competes for the same public wonder. Elliotson's pages treat the older mesmeric gospel as the true key. The thirteen volume set preserves the English movement from 1843 to 1856. Volume nine shows its ninth year of stubborn print. Few fringe sciences left so full a record. The detail here is dense and direct.
smith-pearl-great-price-1851:
Franklin D. Richards published the first Pearl of Great Price at Liverpool in 1851, a slim pamphlet with lasting weight. He gathered pieces of Joseph Smith's work for British Saints who lacked the American prints and papers. Extracts from the Book of Moses and the Book of Abraham stand at its heart, word for word.

Smith's own history and the Articles of Faith, his crisp list of beliefs, complete the little book for its first readers. What began as a missionary pamphlet grew into one of Mormonism's four standard works in time. The 1851 edition shows that scripture in embryo, before canonization fixed its place in the church.
fielding-amelia-1751:
Amelia, published in 1751, was Fielding's last novel, and his most serious. It draws on the troubles of his own first marriage and his years as a London magistrate. Many readers rank its heroine among the finest women in early fiction.

Amelia Booth stays loyal to her husband Billy, a charming, weak ex-officer ruined by debt, drink, and prison. Fielding shows the sponging houses, bailiffs, and corrupt courts that ground the poor of London. The tone is tender and angry at once. Amelia sold more slowly than Tom Jones, but later critics, Dickens among them, praised its truth and pathos.
firmicus-maternus-mathesis-latin-1551:
Julius Firmicus Maternus wrote Rome's fullest handbook of the stars in the fourth century. Mathesis, in the Latin printing of 1551, gives his eight books in their old form. The 1551 edition is a fine Renaissance print of a late Roman work.

Firmicus teaches the whole art of casting a birth chart: planets, houses, lots, and the fates read from them. He mixes hard rules with praise of the star craft and scorn for its frauds. No Latin book of astrology to survive matches its scope. The old print lets readers meet the work as Renaissance scholars did.
plos-pone-0003451:
Jochen Maurer and co-authors compared mouse and human stem cells in this 2008 paper. Both kinds of embryonic stem cells are workhorses of lab research. Gene data hinted they differ in keratins, proteins that form inner cell scaffolds. The team checked those hints at the RNA and protein level.

The contrast held up in the cells themselves. Human and mouse stem cells switched on different keratin sets. That gap may mark a basic difference between the two cell types. It warns against assuming mouse stem cell results apply directly to humans.
plos-pone-0003551:
Yu-Fang Pei and co-authors compared ways to fill gaps in gene data in this 2008 paper. Missing genotypes weaken genetic association studies. Researchers can impute, or infer, untyped markers from typed neighbors. Known linkage patterns between markers make that inference possible.

The team analyzed the accuracy of different imputation methods. Each method was tested on how well it recovered hidden variants. Accuracy gaps matter for replication studies done on computers. Their comparison guides gene hunters toward methods that hold up. Inferred data now fill most large gene banks used by labs worldwide.
plos-pone-0003651:
Elena M. Lucchetta, Meghan E. Vincent, and Rustem F. Ismagilov published this embryo study in PLOS ONE in 2008. In fruit fly embryos, a protein called Bicoid forms a gradient that helps set the head-to-tail pattern. Textbooks treat that gradient as a precise map the embryo reads.

The team tested whether the map must be exact during division cycles 11 to 13. Patterning still came out precise even when the gradient was not exact at those steps. Their result suggests the embryo can tolerate loose input at this stage. Final body precision, it seems, does not require precision at every earlier step.
plos-pone-0003751:
Yelda A. Leal, Laura L. Flores, Laura B. García-Cortés, and colleagues published this meta-analysis in PLOS ONE in 2008. Helicobacter pylori is a stomach bacterium that infects many children. Antibody blood tests can detect it, and designs such as ELISA and Western blot compete. Poorer countries need the cheaper option to work.

The authors pooled studies of antibody-based tests for infection in children. Their combined verdict weighs how well each test design performs. The result guides which test clinics should trust when young patients need a diagnosis and lab resources are thin.
plos-pone-0003851:
Chuancheng Ren, Xuwen Gao, Gang Niu, and colleagues published this stroke study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Briefly interrupting blood flow just after it returns, called postconditioning, can shrink stroke damage in rats. The catch is timing: protection seemed to demand action within seconds or minutes of reperfusion.

The team tested delayed postconditioning against focal ischemic brain injury in rats. Even with the delay, the treatment protected the brain. Extending the window matters, because a therapy that only works in the first minute can rarely reach patients in real hospitals. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008.
plos-pone-0003951:
De-Hua Yu, James Macdonald, Guohong Liu, and co-authors revisited an old worm drug as a cancer agent in 2008. Pyrvinium pamoate has long treated intestinal worms in people. The team found it blocks free-floating cancer cell growth far more than anchored growth. Others had reported anti-tumor effects in living animals too.

Their PLOS ONE article links pyrvinium to the unfolded protein response under low sugar. Stressed cancer cells lean on that response to survive. Pairing pyrvinium with other therapy raised its anti-tumor activity. An approved old drug with a new use could reach trials faster.
plos-pone-0004051:
Marta Mendiola, Jorge Barriuso, Andrés Redondo, and co-authors profiled vessel genes in ovarian cancer in 2008. Ovarian carcinoma is the top gynecological cancer killer in Western societies. Standard chemotherapy pairs paclitaxel with carboplatin. Most advanced cases still relapse after treatment.

Their PLOS ONE article measured genes tied to angiogenesis, the growth of blood vessels. A gene profile carried prognostic value independent of other factors. Tumors feed themselves by growing vessels, so the profile tracks aggression. Such a profile could help sort patients by likely outcome. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004151:
Wei Hu and colleagues published this drug delivery study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Minocycline is an antibiotic pill that reaches the brain well. It also blocks MMP-9, an enzyme tied to inflammation, and it eases disease in an animal model of multiple sclerosis called EAE.

The team packaged minocycline inside liposomes, tiny fat bubbles coated with PEG to help them circulate longer. They tested whether this packaged form calms autoimmune disease in the central nervous system better than the plain drug. The work explores a delivery trick that could make an old drug work harder against brain inflammation.
plos-pone-0004251:
Stefano Tiziani and colleagues published this leukaemia study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Two drugs, bezafibrate and medroxyprogesterone acetate, show unexpected activity against acute myeloid leukaemia when combined. That activity is tied to the generation of reactive oxygen species inside the tumour cells.

The team used metabolomic profiling, a broad survey of small molecules in the cells, to map how leukaemia cell lines respond to the drugs. Charting the chemistry of the response helps explain why the drug pair works. It may also reveal which patients' cells are most likely to answer.
plos-pone-0004351:
Derryck Klarkowski and colleagues published this HIV testing study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Concerns about false-positive HIV results led to a review of testing procedures. The review covered a Médecins Sans Frontières HIV programme in Bukavu, in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. The programme used the WHO two-test rapid diagnostic algorithm, where two positive rapid tests alone diagnose HIV.

The team evaluated a rapid in situ HIV confirmation test in this programme, which had a high failure rate under the standard algorithm. Confirming positives on the spot protects patients from a wrong, life-changing diagnosis.
plos-pone-0004451: In 2009, Azam, Leong, and Zarafshar found shape alone deciding self-assembly. Compactness determined whether tiny cubes and octahedrons self-assembled neatly. The tighter tiles clicked neatly into place. The simple rule guides tiny nanofabrication. The neat study spans atomic to macro scales.
plos-pone-0004551: In 2009, Carrara, Zwang, and Ashley tracked malaria drugs slowly losing punch. Treatment responses to artesunate-mefloquine on Thailand's northwestern border were reviewed. The drug combo faltered over the years. The finding warns of growing resistance. The target malaria was deadly falciparum.
plos-pone-0004651: In 2009, two scientists built a neat math model of attention's spotlight. The model showed how focus boosts brain cells firing. The model explained the boost neatly and fully. The neat paper informs vision science today. The mental spotlight is selective.
plos-pone-0004751: In 2009, a team found protein scissors shaping beetle growth and defense anew here. The cutters steered both growth and defense in beetles anew. The cutters did double duty well. The study maps beetle wiring today. The cutter tools are ancient indeed.
anzus-treaty-1951:
Australia, New Zealand, and the United States signed the ANZUS security treaty at San Francisco in 1951. The pact was sealed while the Korean War raged and fear of communist expansion ran high across the Pacific. Australia and New Zealand also wanted an American promise of protection as they accepted a lenient peace with Japan.

Under the terms, each party must act to meet a common danger if another party is attacked in the Pacific area. The three also promise to consult whenever one of them feels threatened. The treaty anchored the American alliance system in the South Pacific. Ties between the United States and New Zealand later frayed over nuclear ship visits, but the pact still frames regional security.
brown-essays-on-characteristics-1751:
John Brown's Essays on the Characteristics appeared in 1751, aimed at the Earl of Shaftesbury, the most polished thinker of the age. Shaftesbury's Characteristics had taught that taste and good humor could ground morals without revealed religion. Brown, a young clergyman, judged that teaching a danger to faith and public virtue.

The essays charge that Shaftesbury's easy deism saps the roots of both religion and morals. Brown answers wit with argument, testing the earl's claims about virtue, ridicule, and human nature. The orthodox reply made its author famous almost overnight and drew him into print wars with other defenders of Shaftesbury. The book captures a key Enlightenment quarrel: whether manners and taste alone can hold a society together.
cia-0000008651:
Death and capture struck two Americans from a US Navy plane downed in Yen Hung district, a January 1975 report records. Yen Hung lies in Quang Ninh province, in North Vietnam's northeast corner. By 1975, American combat operations had been over for two years.

Late reports like this one reached back to losses that the war's end had left unresolved. One man dead and one captured, if confirmed, split a case file into grief and continued searching. The entry shows the accounting still active in the war's final year. Its facts came through channels that kept working after the shooting stopped.
cia-0000009451:
Francis Gary Powers and the board of inquiry into his case form the subject of an untitled CIA report from January 1962. Powers piloted the U-2 spy plane shot down over the Soviet Union in May 1960. His capture and trial in Moscow caused a worldwide crisis.

A board of inquiry meant the agency examining its own man's conduct and its own decisions. Had Powers followed orders? Could the flight have been avoided? Weeks after this report, Powers came home in a prisoner swap. The file preserves the agency's self-examination at the height of the Cold War's most famous spy case.
cia-0000012251:
Bonn's course between Washington and Paris was the puzzle in a CIA paper from March 1965 on West German foreign policy. Chancellor Ludwig Erhard led a state that owed its safety to the American alliance. Yet France's de Gaulle courted Bonn toward a more independent Europe, and the pull ran both ways.

The paper weighs Erhard's compass: Atlantic loyalty against French invitations. It also judges Bonn's stance toward the Soviet bloc and the divided Germany it claimed to speak for. The study shows the Federal Republic's diplomacy at a crossroads, read closely by the ally it could not leave.
cia-0000013851: Wounded American troops had to be lifted off the battlefield, and a CIA note dated May 5, 1967, covers that work. Getting hurt men out fast was a hard, risky task in Vietnam. Rescue teams faced fire, bad weather, and rough ground. The note preserves a small piece of the war's rescue effort, seen from the files of the time.
cia-0000015251: An unidentified flying object was seen on the Iran and USSR border, in a CIA report dated July 2, 1957. Border sightings drew extra care, since no side owned the sky there. A light or craft over a tense line could mean a probe, a plane, or a mistake. The report files the sighting for the watch on Soviet skies.
cia-0000015351: Names of outside experts tapped as consultants for an advisory panel on unidentified flying objects fill a CIA item dated January 5, 1953. The panel was being formed as saucer reports pressed in from across the country. Scientists lent their names and judgment to a subject many colleagues scorned. Who agreed to serve mattered, since the panel's standing would shape how its findings were received.
cia-0000022651: Two American prisoners of war were sighted in Tan Uyen District, in Bien Hoa Province, a CIA record dated in 1972 reports. Bien Hoa, northeast of Saigon, held a major American air base in war years. A sighting so close to old friendly ground stung the men who kept the lists. It was checked like all the rest, name by name.
cia-0000023651: Allende's election is the whole subject of a CIA document dated in 1970. Salvador Allende won Chile's presidency that September, the first Marxist to do so by vote in the region. Washington watched the result with deep alarm, as other Chile files of the time show. A document titled this plainly holds the first draft of a crisis that ran for years.
cia-0000036851:
An FBIS dispatch dated September 2, 1967 notes McCain as one of many pilots downed over Hanoi. It adds that he came from the carrier Oriskany, which flew strikes off Vietnam. The dispatch places one famous loss inside the much larger air war.

Readers see the pilot's capture framed by numbers: many planes, many men, one city. That framing is itself evidence of how the air war's cost was reported. The file keeps both the man and the scale of the campaign that brought him down. Carrier pilots flew again and again over the same defended city, and the losses mounted month by month.
cia-0000037151:
Claimed sightings of American personnel still missing in action in Laos fill a CIA record dated June 4, 1982. The sightings look back to the period from 1969 onward, when the war in Laos was at its height. Laos held many missing men whose fates were never settled during the war.

The record gathers the claims so they can be weighed together rather than one by one. Grouped sightings sometimes lined up into a pattern, and sometimes fell apart under checking. Either way, the file shows the Laos cases still open and active more than a decade after the fighting there had ended.
cia-0000044451:
A Jesuit leader spoke on the killing of the priests, in a CIA record dated October 4, 1989 in the catalog. The leader spoke for the order that had lost six of its own. His words carried grief and authority in equal measure that autumn.

Inside, the order's public answer to the murders is preserved. The Jesuits had served El Salvador's poor and its university for years. Their leader had to mourn his brothers and answer for their work. The file holds that double task in his own words, at the moment when the order's loss was newest and its future in the country least sure.
cia-0000045251:
Further word on Rey Prendes's September 25 news conference fills a CIA record dated August 5, 1985 in the catalog. The catalog date sits oddly before the conference it names. Follow-up items chased a hard-liner's public performance that autumn.

Inside, more of the right-wing leader's case is set down. News conferences by men like Rey Prendes were aimed at Duarte. They warned him, in public, against softness toward the rebels. The file preserves the follow-up echoes of that warning, part of the pressure that hemmed the president in while he bargained for his daughter's life.
cia-0000049051: Salvadoran armed forces officers gave their views on the possible arrest of a lieutenant in a CIA item from 1983. Arresting one of their own was the test the officer corps resisted most, and their reactions map that resistance. The item survives among the records later gathered for the Truth Commission.
cia-0000049151: New developments in the investigation of the Jesuit murders fill a partly blacked-out CIA item from 1990. The case against the soldiers who killed six priests moved in public steps and private ones, and the blacked-out lines hide the private half. The item survives in the Truth Commission files.
cia-0000049251: A government investigation of killings in El Salvador is the subject of a CIA item from 1989, kept with the Truth Commission records. frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1251:
Hurley wrote to the President and the Secretary of State on 26 July 1945. The date was heavy with news: Britain's count changed its government that day, and the Allies issued their terms to Japan. Hurley's dispatch from China entered that stream at the top level.

His reports kept China's crisis before the men who could act on it. The republic he dealt with was fraying as victory neared, and his cables said so in his own blunt style. This message is one of his summit-week reports. It shows the China file claiming its share of the leaders' crowded day.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1351:
Norman Armour, the American ambassador in Spain, answered the acting secretary of state on 18 July 1945. Two days earlier, Washington had sent Armour fresh instructions. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

An ambassador's reply shows how guidance from home plays out on the ground. Armour dealt with Franco's Spain, a state the winning powers kept at arm's length while still needing to talk. Read with the instruction that came before it, this cable forms a small pair: order and report, question and answer. Pairs like that are the basic rhythm of the whole Foreign Relations series.
frus-1945-50-intel-d51:
Harold Smith, the budget director, wrote to President Truman again on 28 November 1945. Smith's letters to the president form one of the volume's strongest threads. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

By late November, Smith was steering the intelligence plan toward its final form. It would be a small central group serving the president and the departments, not a giant new spy agency. His memoranda combined advice on structure with the drafts themselves. Readers who want to know why the outcome of January 1946 looked as it did should read Smith's papers with care. Few officials leave so clear a trail from their desk to a president's signature.
frus-1945-50-intel-d151:
On 9 May 1946 the Fourth Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board sat, and the minutes of the session survive here. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 151 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The postwar system was still new: the National Intelligence Authority gave the orders, and the Central Intelligence Group carried them out.

Minutes are the formal record of a meeting: who sat in, what was put on the table, and what the group agreed to do. They rarely give long speeches, but they fix the choices that later memos then carry out. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d251:
A memorandum dated 2 December 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Deputy Director of Central Intelligence (Wright). The reader was the Chief of the Interagency Coordinating and Planning Staff, Central Intelligence Agency (Childs). It stands as document 251 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. A new order was taking shape: the National Security Council now met at the top, with the CIA as its intelligence arm.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d351: Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter issued a formal statement on 31 August 1948. It is document 351 in the Foreign Relations volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. A signed statement put the head of the CIA on record in his own name. At the time, an outside team was set to review how the young agency worked.
frus-1861-d51:
On 8 June 1861, William H. Seward sent a brief letter to Charles Francis Adams in London. The letter is document 51 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward sent Adams frequent, brief direction through the summer of 1861. Each letter dealt with the point then at hand, from notes to claims. This June note is one stroke in a run of orders that kept London's envoy and Washington's chief in close step despite the slow mails. Brief orders suited Adams, who liked clear tasks and disliked loose talk in state papers. Clear tasks also let Adams answer fast when a point turned hot in talks.
frus-1861-d151:
William Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 September 1861. The dispatch is document 151 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Dayton's early September report keeps the Paris watch at its steady pace. He had learned the court's moods and could read small signs. Washington drew on that feel when it judged how far French patience with the war might stretch. Feel for a court cannot be taught by cable, and Dayton had it in full. Feel for a court is the one tool no office at home could supply by mail.
frus-1861-d251:
The home office spoke to James Shepherd Pike on 5 September 1861, through a letter from Seward. It stands as Document 251 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d51:
From abroad on 24 April 1862, Charles Francis Adams sent Seward his latest account. It stands as Document 51 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It was written in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d151:
From London on 25 September 1862, Charles Francis Adams reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. Adams was the American minister to Britain, and his reports home appear throughout the 1862 Foreign Relations volume; this one is Document 151.

An envoy's report mixed what he had done, what officials had said to him, and what the press and public seemed to think. Seward read these London letters to judge the risk that Britain might back the Confederacy or push for a truce. Reports like this one were the government's eyes in the capital that mattered most. Earl Russell, the British foreign secretary, was the minister Adams dealt with most in London.
frus-1862-d251:
On 3 February 1862 William L. Dayton wrote from Paris to Secretary of State William H. Seward, in a report printed as Document 251 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton had served as American minister to France since 1861.

Early February brought the fall of Fort Henry in Tennessee, the first big Union win of the year. Such news mattered in Paris, where bets on the war's length guided French choices. Dayton's reports mixed court talk with press and market reaction, giving Seward the raw material for his replies to the French legation in Washington. France's Mexican venture shared the court's attention with the American war all year.
frus-1862-d351:
From Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward closed the year with a letter to Henri Mercier dated 31 December 1861, printed as Document 351 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Mercier was France's minister in Washington.

New Year's Eve 1861 found the Trent crisis settled and French, British, and Spanish troops landing in Mexico. Seward faced a year ahead in which France would test American patience on two fronts. His year-end letter to Mercier is a fitting close to the French file's first chapter: courteous in form, careful in substance. Seward tested what Mercier said against what Dayton reported from Paris, week by week.
frus-1862-d451:
On 17 February 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to John Lothrop Motley at the legation in Vienna. The instruction is Document 451 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's printed record.

February brought Union victories at Fort Henry and Fort Donelson, and Seward was quick to put such news in his ministers' hands. Motley in Vienna had to counter a court press that often took the Confederacy's side. Orders from Washington gave him the facts and the argument: the rebellion was failing, and foreign backing for it would be wasted. The letter is one move in the paper campaign the Union fought in every European capital that winter.
frus-1862-d551:
Roest van Limburg wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 October 1862. His note is Document 551 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

October brought the Dutch minister a Washington calmer than September's, with Lee back in Virginia and the intervention scare cooling. Van Limburg's note took up the standing business of his legation, which centered on Dutch trade and the treatment of neutral shipping. The Netherlands file in the volume never rises to crisis, and that is its historical value. It records the normal temperature of relations between the Union and a friendly maritime power. It does so in the middle of a civil war.
frus-1862-d651:
Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this letter to Townsend Harris on 23 July 1861. Harris was the American minister in Japan, the man who had won the 1858 trade treaty with the shogun's court. The letter is document 651 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Seward's letters to his envoys carried orders, news from home, and the line each post was to take. This one went out in the first summer of the Civil War, when Washington had few men and little money to spare for far-off posts. It shows the State Department still steering its Japan mission week by week, even with a war on.

The evidence gives the date and the spot in the run, but no title, no writer, and no one addressed.
frus-1863p1-d151:
Charles Francis Adams closed his mail day with this third dispatch of 9 April 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 151 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The third sheet of a set often sent the day's last facts or a name to note for the files. Adams's close of 9 April sits in that place. His April letters, read whole, chart the weeks when Britain first curbed the South's shipbuilding in earnest. This one is the tail of a day's work in that turn, plain in tone and firm in its facts.
frus-1863p1-d251: Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Charles Francis Adams, his minister in London, on 28 July 1863. Secretary of State William H. Seward received a letter dated 7 April 1863 from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d551:
In the flow of wartime mail, Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons wrote to William H. Seward, Secretary of State on 5 June 1863. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the early summer of 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d651:
On 30 October 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Mail between London and Washington crossed the Atlantic by steamer, so each reply took weeks to complete the round trip. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
plos-pbio-0000051:
Anthony M. Giannetti, Peter M. Snow, Olga Zak, and co-workers published this study in PLOS Biology in 2003. It asks how the human transferrin receptor can bind more than one partner. That receptor sits on cell surfaces and pulls iron into cells by catching transferrin, the blood protein that carries iron.

A receptor that must catch iron-loaded transferrin, let go at the right time, and still deal with other binders needs a neat trick. The authors work out the shape and contact points that let one receptor handle these jobs. The result helps explain how cells control iron intake. That process matters for blood health. It also matters in diseases where iron builds up or runs short.
plos-pbio-0020351:
Richard W. R. Retallick, Hamish McCallum, and Rick Speare surveyed a frog disease in Australia in PLOS Biology in 2004. A fungus called chytrid has driven sharp frog declines worldwide. The team checked a frog community after its decline, to see whether the fungus was still present.

It was: the fungus persisted at low levels in the surviving frogs, a state called endemic infection. That finding changes the recovery picture. Frogs that remain are not free of the threat; they live with it. Some species may have gained tolerance, while others stay rare. For conservation, the message is that saving such communities means managing a lasting disease, not waiting for it to pass.
plos-pone-0000151:
Claudia Hetzer, Dwayne Bisgrove, Michael S. Cohen, and colleagues published this HIV study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It examines how the viral protein Tat recruits and switches on RSK2, an enzyme inside human cells. Tat is the protein HIV uses to drive production of more virus from an infected cell.

By tracing Tat's grip on RSK2, the authors map one step in HIV's takeover of cell machinery. Each such step is a possible place for a drug to intervene. The paper adds detail to the picture of how the virus borrows host enzymes, knowledge that antiviral design depends on.
plos-pone-0000251:
Dario L. Ringach published this theoretical neuroscience paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It asks where the functional architecture of the cortex comes from. These are the orderly maps in the brain's outer layer, where neighboring neurons respond to similar features of the world. The author proposes an account of how that organization originates.

Cortical maps are among the most striking patterns in the brain, and their origin has been debated for decades. The paper argues for a developmental explanation rooted in the statistics of input and wiring. It is a theory piece, meant to organize data and provoke tests, rather than report a new experiment.
plos-pone-0000351:
Jules B. Panksepp, Kimberly A. Jochman, Joseph U. Kim, and colleagues published this mouse behavior paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Adolescent mice vary genetically in how social they are. The authors report that affiliative behavior, ultrasonic communication, and social reward are all influenced by genetic variation in these young mice.

Mice talk ultrasonically and find company rewarding, much as social mammals do. Showing genes sway those traits makes the mouse a model for the biology of sociability. The work is relevant to research on conditions marked by social differences, where genetic effects are strong but hard to study in people.
plos-pone-0000451:
Sukanya Narasimhan and colleagues vaccinated against tick saliva itself, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The black-legged tick Ixodes scapularis spreads Lyme disease, caused by Borrelia bacteria. The team targeted salivary proteins the tick injects within 24 hours of attachment, aiming to build immunity against those early proteins.

The title states the strategy worked: immunity thwarted tick feeding and impaired Borrelia transmission. A vaccine that stops the tick from feeding could block several tick-borne diseases at once, not just one germ. The study supports anti-tick vaccines as a different line of defense, aimed at the carrier rather than the disease.
plos-pone-0000551:
Scott R. Evans and colleagues tested a drug for HIV-related nerve pain with the help of an electronic diary, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. HIV-associated sensory neuropathies cause burning pain in the feet and hands. Their randomized trial evaluated Prosaptide for this condition, while patients recorded neuropathic pain in an electronic diary rather than from memory at clinic visits.

Pain is subjective and fades in recall, so real-time diaries measure a drug's effect more honestly. A randomized trial built on such records sets a higher standard for pain claims. Even the measurement method here is part of the contribution to a difficult field.
plos-pone-0000651:
Pengyuan Liu, Haris Vikis, Yan Lu and co-authors mapped complex traits in mice by computer, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Understanding the genetics of common diseases and their measurable traits should aid diagnostics and treatments. Mice offer rich genome and trait data gathered in many separate resources. Bringing those resources together quickly could speed gene discovery.

Their approach is in silico mapping at large scale, meaning computation across inbred mouse strains rather than new breeding. Inbred strains differ in known ways, so trait differences can be matched to genome differences. A validated shortcut like this saves years, and its hits point biologists to candidate genes for lab testing.
plos-pone-0000751:
Tara G. Martin, Iadine Chadès, Peter Arcese and colleagues asked how to spend conservation money on animals that will not stay put. Migratory species make up a significant portion of the world's biodiversity, and annual conservation investment in them exceeds several billion dollars. Designing effective plans is enormously challenging, because migrants are influenced by events across whole routes and seasons.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE study seeks the optimal conservation of migratory species. Optimal means deciding where protection buys the most survival: breeding grounds, wintering grounds, or the stops between. A species can be guarded carefully in one country and lost in another. This work frames that allocation as a solvable problem.

The team studied sick cells, and healthy cells dosed with a drug that copies the defect.

They tracked how the buildup changes the endosome membrane and slows traffic within it. Their title states the result plainly: the buildup leads to impaired intra-endosomal trafficking. If sorting stalls, the cell starves amid plenty. That jam helps explain the wide cell damage seen in this disease.

The team call the pattern ankyrin-B syndrome. The variants enhance cardiac function yet carry a risk of cardiac death and early senescence, cell aging. One version of the theory says that whether rival males are close kin should change that choice.
